subject: Alphabet's worst day ever, Amazon's $77B quarter
bodyMarkdown:
If you hold a Canadian index fund or a target date fund in your RRSP, three companies that make up a large slice of it reported this week, and one of them lost about $500 billion of value in a single session on Thursday. The spending that the market cheered all year is now the thing it is selling.

## What the three of them reported

Microsoft and Alphabet both reported on Wednesday evening, Amazon after the close last night. Microsoft's Azure revenue grew 48 per cent, ahead of its own guidance, and the stock rose. Alphabet spent $51.36 billion on capital projects in the quarter, more than double a year earlier, and still came in under the $55.09 billion analysts had modelled. Google Cloud revenue doubled, up 103 per cent. Then Amazon went the other way entirely, with capital spending of $77.3 billion in one quarter against $35.1 billion a year earlier, and against a FactSet estimate of $58.7 billion. AWS grew 39 per cent to roughly $46 billion, its fastest in nearly five years, on a reported backlog of $578 billion. Amazon's revenue was $201.9 billion and its operating margin reached a record 13.9 per cent. Both Alphabet and Amazon fell.

## Why Alphabet got hit hardest

CNBC reported on Thursday that Alphabet dropped 13 per cent, its worst day ever, shedding around $500 billion in market value. The number that did the damage sits lower down the statement. **Free cash flow**, the cash a business has left once it has paid for both its operations and its buildings and equipment, came in at negative $9.07 billion where analysts had pencilled in positive $2.7 billion, and it was the second negative quarter in a row. Alphabet's CFO put it down to capital spending, an inventory build for TPU system sales, and the European Commission fine the company paid. Now hold that beside Amazon, which overshot its spending estimate by nearly $19 billion, fell about 6 per cent after hours, and reported trailing twelve month free cash flow of negative $42.4 billion. Underspend and you get sold. Overspend and you get sold.

## The bottleneck moved from money to chips

Microsoft's shortfall is the one I find most telling, because it was not a choice. Capital spending came in at $45.2 billion including finance leases, against analyst estimates near $50.7 billion, and CFO Amy Hood said third party GPU suppliers had run late, pushing some usable capacity out into the first half of 2027. That is a company that wanted to spend more and could not get the hardware. It reads differently next to what SK hynix told investors on Wednesday, that long term agreements with 14 customers already cover more than half its capacity for 2027 and 2028. The firms renting that hardware out took the news badly. TipRanks reported CoreWeave down about 6 per cent and Nebius about 7 per cent in Thursday's premarket, because Microsoft buys capacity from these **neoclouds**, companies that do nothing but rent AI computing by the hour. The Nasdaq closed 1.38 per cent lower.

## The takeaway

Watch free cash flow rather than the capex headline as the remaining reports land. If Amazon holds near $220 billion of spending for 2026 and goes meaningfully higher in 2027 as it said last night, and if Andy Jassy's call for AWS growth above 40 per cent in 2027 and 2028 comes good, the money will have been well spent. If AWS growth slips below that while the cash keeps draining, this week will read as the point where the market began asking for receipts. I would not rebalance an RRSP around one bad Thursday, but I would go and find out how much of my portfolio sits in these four names, because most Canadians hold more of them than they think.
